India’s inflation hits near two-year high of 5.54% in September, backing RBI’s rate hike

Retail inflation rose from 4.83% in August, driven by food prices and rising costs, as a weaker rupee and elevated oil prices add to pressure on the RBI.

Anup Roy  and  Asmi Bhatia

12 October, 2026 09:29 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Market stalls in Mumbai, India, on Sunday, Aug. 9, 2026. | Bloomberg

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

India’s inflation accelerated to an almost two-year high in September, nearing the top of the central bank’s 2% to 6% tolerance band and reinforcing its decision to lift interest rates last week for the first time in almost four years.

The consumer price index rose 5.54% last month from a year earlier, the highest since late-2024 and up from a revised 4.83% in August, data released Monday by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation showed. That was broadly in-line with the 5.58% median estimate in a Bloomberg survey of economists.

Indian government bonds held onto losses after the release, with the benchmark 10-year yield trading around 10 basis points higher at 7.40%. The rupee is up 1% on Monday though it remains one of the worst-performing currencies in Asia to-date.

Show Full Article

The combination of rising inflation and a weaker currency is particularly challenging for the country’s central bank as a falling rupee makes imports more expensive just as price pressures are broadening. The RBI expects inflation to average 6% in the three months through December and raised its full-year forecast to 5.2%.

Monday’s reading comes just days after the Reserve Bank of India’s monetary policy committee voted unanimously to raise its benchmark rate by 25 basis points to 5.50% and shifted its stance to “calibrated tightening.”

“Amid continued stickiness in commodity prices, and rising global yields, we expect RBI to continue to remain firmly on path of rate hikes,” said Garima Kapoor, economist at Elara Securities. She sees two more rate increases by end-March.

September’s acceleration was driven largely by food inflation, which climbed to 7.74% from 5.97% in August. The category makes up more than a third of the retail inflation basket, and deficient rainfall is expected to add to price pressures in coming months.

Elevated global oil prices remain a worry. The government has largely shielded consumers from the increase at the pump, raising retail fuel prices only modestly in May even as crude has climbed back above $100 a barrel.

Businesses have still felt the squeeze. Higher food and energy costs have raised their expenses and eroded margins, with producers so far absorbing much of the increase rather than passing it on to consumers.

“A broad-based food shock is more persistent and carries a greater risk of feeding into household inflation expectations than a temporary increase in vegetable prices,” said Kunal Kundu, economist with Societe Generale, in a note.

Monday’s figures also showed:

Transport costs climbed 5.01% from a year earlier, compared with 4.6% in August.

Restaurant and hotel prices rose 9.36%, compared with 8.38% a month earlier.

Personal care prices advanced 13.75%, compared with 15.17% in August.

–With assistance from Bhaskar Dutta.

What Trump’s Russian diesel deal means for US, surging global prices & Indian refiners

The US has eased sanctions on Russian diesel to address fuel-price pressures, raising questions over its Russia policy and the outlook for Indian refiners.

Udit Bubna

12 October, 2026 06:27 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

File photo of Russian President Vladimir Putin with his American counterpart Donald Trump | Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: US President Donald Trump’s decision to bring Russian diesel back into the American market has raised questions about Washington’s sanctions policy against Moscow and its efforts to curb revenues funding the war in Ukraine.

Trump’s decision comes ahead of the November mid-term elections, with diesel prices near record levels. Diesel is essential for trucking, agriculture and heating in the US, making higher fuel costs a concern for households and businesses.

The announcement on Friday came less than a month after Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which provides for tariffs of up to 100 percent on goods from countries that continue to buy Russian oil and gas under specified conditions.

Show Full Article

On 9 October, the US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued General License 135, temporarily authorising specified transactions involving Russian-origin diesel until 7 April 2027, allowing the proposed trade to proceed.

However, analysts are sceptical that the additional volumes will significantly ease global diesel shortages or bring down prices across markets.

Abu Dhabi-based commodity analyst Natalia Katona said the arrangement appeared to be directed at a specific regional market rather than the global diesel shortage. “The US Atlantic coast, particularly New York and the wider Northeast, has a persistent diesel shortfall because it lacks sufficient refining capacity.” .

Regular seaborne imports of around 200,000-300,000 barrels per day help meet that shortfall, Katona said.

“While many in the market argue that these volumes won’t solve the global diesel shortage, Trump is addressing a very specific local problem: diesel prices in the traditionally Democratic Northeast ahead of the elections,” she told ThePrint.

Also Read: India’s now importing pre-conflict levels of Gulf crude; share of Russian oil lowest since April

Sanctions relief versus pressure on Russia Trump’s move highlights the contrast between the US easing restrictions on its own proposed Russian diesel imports and threatening penalties against other major buyers of Russian energy.

America-based energy strategist and geopolitical analyst Umud Shokri said the arrangement was administratively permitted under the US licence, but actual deliveries would depend on available Russian supplies, export rules, shipping and payment arrangements. He also noted that some US lawmakers had questioned whether the move conflicted with federal law.

Russia’s own restrictions could pose another constraint. Moscow extended its diesel export ban for producers until 31 October, citing the need to stabilise domestic fuel supplies. Meanwhile, Ukrainian drone attacks continue to disrupt Russian refining capacity.

Despite restrictions on diesel exports, Russia continued supplying some foreign markets during the sanctions period through government-to-government arrangements which was exempt from its export ban, Katona said. These shipments included supplies to Mongolia, Kyrgyzstan and other Central Asian countries.

Shokri said there was no indication that Russian refineries returned to peak operating levels. In September, half of Russia’s six largest diesel-producing refineries had significantly reduced or halted output following drone damage, he said.

Under Trump’s supply arrangement, Russia is expected to ship 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and one million tonnes in December, according to Katona.

These volumes would be equivalent to around 75,000 barrels per day (b/d), 125,000 b/d and 250,000 b/d, respectively, averaged over a month. The December shipment could cover almost all of the US Northeast’s regular diesel import requirement of 200,000-300,000 b/d.

However, high freight rates and a shortage of clean-product tankers could limit the wider impact, as diesel markets have become increasingly regional.

Russia, according to Katona, last supplied diesel to the US in 2022, with arrivals peaking at 210,000 tonnes in December that year. No cargoes have arrived since 2023.

What it means for India’s oil trade For Indian refiners, the bigger risk lies in changing regional trade flows and potential pressure on export margins rather than direct competition from Russian diesel in the US.

India exported 630,000 barrels per day (b/d) of diesel in September, of which Europe took 280,000 b/d. These shipments had largely been contracted one to two months earlier, Katona said.

The outlook will depend on whether China resumes larger diesel exports and how shipping costs to Europe evolve.

“If China starts flooding the Singapore and Southeast Asian markets, India will have no option other than to re-orient flows towards East Africa and Europe,” Katona said.

China’s planned return to diesel exports has already pushed down refining margins in Singapore to $64-65 per barrel, she added. If shipping costs to Europe remain high, Indian refiners may find it more profitable to sell their diesel in Asian markets instead.

Shokri said a possible recovery in Russian diesel production and exports could increase competition for Indian fuel, particularly in Europe, where shipments grew in September. The greater availability of Russian diesel could narrow price premiums and compress Indian refiners’ margins, he said.

The scale of the impact will depend on how much Russia can produce and export, given continuing refinery damage and export restrictions.

For India, the key variables are Chinese exports, Russian supply, regional diesel margins and freight rates. These factors will determine where Indian fuel can be sold most profitably as shifting trade flows and sanctions reshape the global diesel market.

(Edited by Tony Rai)

Surfing hotspots around the world are more vulnerable to climate change, says new study

The research analysed 57 surf breaks across eight countries to arrive at its findings. Each of the sites selected is incorporated into a World Surfing Reserve.

Purvi Rajpuria

12 October, 2026 04:43 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Representative image (c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2024

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: Many of the most prominent surf breaks across the world are vulnerable to climate change, even as the degree and type of vulnerability differ widely, a recent study found.

The study, titled ‘ Globally significant surf breaks are vulnerable to climate change ’, was co-authored by Dan R Reineman of California State University Channel Islands, along with researchers from Save The Waves Coalition and World Surfing Reserves .

The research analysed 57 surf breaks across eight countries to arrive at its findings. Each of the sites selected is incorporated into a World Surfing Reserve (WSR)—“a status applied for by local stakeholders and designated by an international non-profit organization based on each site’s cultural, historical, and environmental significance for surfing,” the study explains.

Show Full Article

These surf breaks, the research found, are vulnerable to climate change, due to changing tide levels, hardened shorelines caused by manmade structures, and shifting sands. Surf breaks rated at most risk include Croyde beach in north Devon, UK, and Oriente Salvaje in El Salvador.

What are surf breaks? Dan Reineman, a co-author of the study, pointed to the several factors that come together to form a surf break. “Surf breaks are incredibly unique oceanographic phenomena – a confluence of all these factors that fit together just right to make the wave happen – and so those processes are really sensitive,” he said .

Some of these factors include swell direction, tide, and intricate combinations of sea-floor shape. Climate change, global warming, and changing rainfall patterns can affect any of these factors, hampering the delicate balance of surf breaks and thus destroying the wave.

Significantly, the study found that coastlines that were more natural and less populated by manmade structures could adapt better to the changes caused by climate change. These coastlines were able to adapt by shifting inland and relocating sediments. Construction of features such as sea walls, jetties and groynes made the beaches and waves less resilient, Reineman said .

Also read: Mamdani has a new target. Subscriptions that make cancellations difficult

Affects local economy at large Climate change-related vulnerability matters not only to surfers, but also to the local people who depend on the multi-billion-dollar surf economy that exists in these sites.

Adam Hall, a co-founder of the North Devon WSR, was one of the local surfers who contributed to the study. Explaining the significance of surfing to the local economy, he said , “Surfers will come throughout the year. They fill up the pubs, restaurants and car parks when the swells are good in January, February and March, where if you go to any other tourist destination that doesn’t have surf, they’re dead on their knees.”

Many of these sites often have little else in terms of local economy.

Local surfers also played a key role in guiding the research. Trent Hodges, a co-author of the study and a senior programmes manager at Save the Waves Coalition, said , “We learned directly from the local surfers how they are seeing their waves change. It’s a canary in the coalmine too – when a wave changes, that often means the beach is changing, and everybody enjoys the beach.”

The study also hypothesises that similar risks could affect other surf breaks, not included in the present research, and encourages other local people and organisations to assess their vulnerability.

(Edited by Ratan Priya)
